Part 1

What is a cause-and-effect matrix, and how do you read one row of it?

Part 1 · the plan

From one sheet to one sentence

  1. What the sheet is forwritten from the HAZOP, used to program the SIS
  2. Anatomy of a rowtag, direction, setting, delay, effects, action codes
  3. Setting and delaywhen a cause acts, and why an alarm comes first
  4. Row → sentenceevery row read aloud as one if-then statement

One page of logic

Rows are causes, columns are effects

A mark where a row and a column cross means “this cause does that”.

Not on this sheet: control loops and valve fail positions on air loss.

Interactive — pick a part of the row

Row 004: PSHH-206 trips K-201

Left half says when, right half says what — a row is complete only when both halves are filled.

Interactive — pick an action code

Sixteen columns, nine action codes

The code sits in the trip-action row above each column.

Valves close or open, machines stop, permissives block — the code is the direction the final element must move.

When does a cause act?

A condition must persist for its delaystep 1 of 2

$c_i$
condition of trip row $i$ (true or false)
–
$\tau_i$
time the condition has been true without a break
s
$d_i$
delay written in the row
s
$\Delta t$
logic scan step of the simulator
0.25 s
$$\tau_i(t+\Delta t)=\begin{cases}\tau_i(t)+\Delta t & c_i\ \text{true}\\[2pt] 0 & c_i\ \text{false}\end{cases}\qquad \text{act when } \tau_i \ge d_i$$

One false scan resets the timer: noise shorter than the delay never trips.

Interactive — pick a row, stretch the upset

Ride through, or tripstep 2 of 2

From the delay ruleact when $\tau_i \ge d_i$

The same 4-s upset trips PSHH-206 but not TSHH-207 — the delay is a filter sized to the process speed.

Interactive — pick a variable

Design, alarm, trip: the order matters

The delay buys seconds; the alarm buys the operator minutes.

Every trip row has its alarm below it on the same variable — a trip with no alarm first gives the operator no chance.

Interactive — pick any row

Read every row as one sentence

If a row cannot be said as one sentence, it is ambiguous — an ambiguous row will be programmed wrongly.

Part 1 · summary

What part 1 settled

  • A C&E is the SIS and alarm logic on one page: rows cause, columns effect.
  • A row: tag, direction, setting, delay; marks and action codes.
  • A cause acts only after its condition holds for the full delay.
  • Alarms sit between design and trip; each row reads as one sentence.

Part 2

What does the matrix of this unit do: which trips, which cascade, which feed shut-off, which permissives?

Part 2 · the plan

Seventy-two rows, sixteen columns

  1. The sheetwhat the 72 rows and 16 columns hold
  2. Reading across and downfilter rows; read a column to see what moves a valve
  3. The cascade interlockone K-201 trip stops two machines
  4. XV-100 and the permissiveswhat cuts the feed, and what must hold to reopen it

RF-CAS-v1-IN-CE-001 · A3, rev R0

One sheet holds the whole cold-end logic

Interactive — filter, then click a row

The matrix, row by row

Only trip rows stop machines or move control valves — alarm rows only alarm, permissive rows only block.

Interactive — pick an effect column

Read down: what moves this element?

Across a row: one cause, many effects. Down a column: one effect, all its causes.

Only three rows close XV-100 — no compressor trip cuts the feed.

Interactive — model run, drag the clock

IS-301: K-201 stops, K-301 follows 3 s later

Nothing condenses the ethylene in E-203 once K-201 stops.

The interlock turns one cause into two machine stops — that is why K-201 rows carry “I” under K-301.

Feed shutdown, latched by the SIS

XV-100: three causes close it, five permissives reopen it

The sheet is a record of the logic as built, gaps included.

Interactive — model run, pick a moment

What blocks a restart?

Twenty minutes after a K-201 trip, K-301 still waits for PI-310 below 14.5 bar a — a permissive encodes the restart procedure.

Part 2 · summary

What part 2 settled

  • 72 rows: 14 trips, PSV-314, 40 alarms, 17 permissives; 16 effect columns.
  • Read across for a cause, down for an effect.
  • IS-301 stops K-301 three seconds after any K-201 stop.
  • Only ESD and the separator LSHH close XV-100; permissives govern every restart.

Part 3

Does the sheet agree with the plant, and how do you prove it?

Part 3 · the plan

Checking the sheet against the simulator

  1. 107 checkssettings, delays, alarms, permissives, effects
  2. Trip replaywhich row lights first, and what follows
  3. Spot the errorwrong cells, and the check that catches each

Like a factory acceptance test, on the model

Five kinds of check, 107 in all

A sheet is trusted only after it has been compared with the logic it describes.

GroupCountC&E compared with
Settings11trip settings in the model
Delays12trip-condition list
Alarms39alarm limits
Permissives3permissive lists
Effects42five tripped copies: what moved

Interactive — pick a group

The checks, one by one

checks agree with the simulator

Effects are checked by tripping copies of the model — a mark is proven only when the element actually moves.

Interactive — model run, no operator action

Which row lights first?

The first-out row names what tripped; alarms before it warned — rows after it are consequences, not causes.

Interactive — pick a variant, click the wrong cell

One cell is wrong in each row

Each error is caught by a check you have seen — compare every cell with the model, not with memory.

Part 3 · summary

What part 3 settled

  • 107 of 107 checks agree: settings, delays, alarms, permissives, effects.
  • In a replay the first-out row names the trip; later rows are consequences.
  • After a K-201 trip the feed stays on and PSV-314 lifts at 22 min.
  • Every planted error is caught by one named check.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Read each row as one sentence: cause, setting, delay, then every marked effect.

2

Check that an alarm sits between design and every trip setting.

3

Read down a column to see what really moves a valve or stops a machine.

4

Find the first-out row before acting on the alarms that follow it.

5

Prove each mark by tripping a copy of the model, not by memory.
